scenes.visual: Title card 'Eight Boxes and a Name' fades in over a cartoon turkey vulture perched on a fence post, its bare red head turned to the camera. THE WORLD, kept for both films: 16:9, pale cream background, flat cartoon animals and plants drawn with a thick dark outline, no molecular structures. COLOUR MAP, the same in every scene and in the second film: one colour per box, deep at the outside and bright at the centre. DOMAIN box = NAVY; KINGDOM = INDIGO; PHYLUM = PURPLE; CLASS = TEAL; ORDER = GREEN; FAMILY = GOLD; GENUS = ORANGE; SPECIES = bright CORAL RED. Each box is a rounded rectangle outline with its level word and group name in a tab on its top edge, in the box's colour. The TURKEY VULTURE is always drawn as a large dark-brown bird with a small bare RED head; the BLACK VULTURE as a dark bird with a bare GREY head; the RED-TAILED HAWK brown with a rust-red tail; the CARDINAL bright red with a crest; the BROOK TROUT olive with pale spots; the BLUE CRAB blue with jointed legs; the PINE TWIG green needles with a small cone. Anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: Who is right when someone calls a vulture a buzzard? Dark birds circle over a Virginia highway. Someone in the car says, look, buzzards! A visitor from Britain looks up for a hawk.
scenes.visual: Cartoon car on a highway under a pale sky; three dark turkey vultures circle above. A speech bubble from the car reads 'Buzzards!'. A second figure with a small British flag badge points up; a thought bubble shows a brown hawk with a feathered head, labelled 'buzzard (in Britain)'. A large question mark appears between the vultures and the hawk and stays on screen.
scenes.narration: Who is right when someone calls a vulture a buzzard? Dark birds circle over a Virginia highway. Someone in the car says, look, buzzards! A visitor from Britain looks up for a hawk.

scenes.tts: Scientists solve this with one name for each kind of living thing. To see where that name comes from, we build boxes, one inside the next.
scenes.visual: The word 'buzzard' sits in the centre with two arrows, one to a turkey vulture and one to the British hawk, labelled 'one word, two birds'. The arrows fade. Seven cartoon living things slide in and line up on the cream floor: pine twig, blue crab, brook trout, cardinal, red-tailed hawk, black vulture, turkey vulture. A few tiny rod-shaped cells drift in at the far left, labelled 'bacteria'.
scenes.narration: Scientists solve this with one name for each kind of living thing. To see where that name comes from, we build boxes, one inside the next.

scenes.tts: Start with one huge box, the domain Eukarya. It holds living things whose cells have a nucleus. All seven fit inside. The bacteria stay outside, because their cells have no nucleus.
scenes.visual: A large NAVY box outline draws itself around the seven living things; its tab reads '1 DOMAIN: Eukarya'. A small inset shows one cartoon cell with a round dot labelled 'nucleus'. The tiny rod-shaped bacteria remain outside the navy box, with a small inset of a cell with no dot, labelled 'no nucleus'. A counter in the top-right corner reads 'boxes: 1'.
scenes.narration: Start with one huge box, the domain Eukarya. It holds living things whose cells have a nucleus. All seven fit inside. The bacteria stay outside, because their cells have no nucleus.

scenes.tts: A smaller box closes inside. This is the kingdom Animalia, the animals. The pine twig is left outside, because plants are another kingdom.
scenes.visual: Inside the navy box, an INDIGO box draws itself around the six animals; its tab reads '2 KINGDOM: Animalia'. The pine twig slides out of the indigo box and stays between the indigo and navy walls, with a small label 'kingdom Plantae'. Counter: 'boxes: 2'.
scenes.narration: A smaller box closes inside. This is the kingdom Animalia, the animals. The pine twig is left outside, because plants are another kingdom.

scenes.tts: Next comes the phylum. Ours is Kor-dah-tah. These animals have a flexible rod and a hollow nerve cord along the back, at least early in life. Fish, birds and people are chordates. The crab has neither, so it is left outside.
scenes.caption: Next comes the phylum. Ours is Chordata. These animals have a flexible rod and a hollow nerve cord along the back, at least early in life. Fish, birds and people are chordates. The crab has neither, so it is left outside.
scenes.visual: A PURPLE box closes around the trout, cardinal, hawk and both vultures; tab '3 PHYLUM: Chordata'. Two faint lines run along the back of the trout and the cardinal, labelled 'flexible rod' and 'hollow nerve cord', with a small grey note 'at least early in life (schematic)'. The blue crab slides out and rests between the purple and indigo walls. Counter: 'boxes: 3'.
scenes.narration: Next comes the phylum. Ours is Chordata. These animals have a flexible rod and a hollow nerve cord along the back, at least early in life. Fish, birds and people are chordates. The crab has neither, so it is left outside.

scenes.tts: The class box is Ay-veez, the birds, so the trout is left outside. Then comes the order. In our database, the order holds hawks, eagles and vultures. The cardinal is left outside.
scenes.caption: The class box is Aves, the birds, so the trout is left outside. Then comes the order. In our database, the order holds hawks, eagles and vultures. The cardinal is left outside.
scenes.visual: A TEAL box closes around the four birds; tab '4 CLASS: Aves'; the trout slides out between teal and purple walls. Then a GREEN box closes around the hawk and both vultures; tab '5 ORDER: Accipitriformes'; a small grey note under the tab reads 'in one database (ITIS)'. The cardinal slides out between green and teal walls. Counter: 'boxes: 5'.
scenes.narration: The class box is Aves, the birds, so the trout is left outside. Then comes the order. In our database, the order holds hawks, eagles and vultures. The cardinal is left outside.

scenes.tts: The family box holds the New World vultures, so the hawk is left outside. Two bare-headed vultures remain.
scenes.visual: A GOLD box closes around the two vultures; tab '6 FAMILY: Cathartidae'. The red-tailed hawk slides out between gold and green walls. Camera pushes in on the two vultures side by side, red head and grey head, inside the gold box. Counter: 'boxes: 6'.
scenes.narration: The family box holds the New World vultures, so the hawk is left outside. Two bare-headed vultures remain.

scenes.tts: The black vulture is in the same family as the turkey vulture. Will it also fit inside the next box, the genus?
scenes.visual: An ORANGE dashed outline hovers above the two vultures, not yet closed, with a tab '7 GENUS: ?'. Text on screen: 'Will the black vulture fit in the genus box too?' A small clock icon appears in the corner.
scenes.narration: The black vulture is in the same family as the turkey vulture. Will it also fit inside the next box, the genus?

scenes.visual: Hold the dashed orange outline above both vultures. Card in the centre: 'Pause and predict: in or out?' A thin countdown bar shrinks over 5 seconds.

scenes.tts: No. Among our seven, the genus box closes around the turkey vulture alone. The black vulture belongs to a different genus, called Kora-jips. It shares six boxes with the turkey vulture, not seven.
scenes.caption: No. Among our seven, the genus box closes around the turkey vulture alone. The black vulture belongs to a different genus, called Coragyps. It shares six boxes with the turkey vulture, not seven.
scenes.visual: The ORANGE box snaps shut around the turkey vulture only; tab '7 GENUS: Cathartes'. The black vulture slides out between orange and gold walls, and a label appears beside it: 'genus Coragyps'. A tally strip under the black vulture lights six coloured squares, navy to gold, with the seventh (orange) and eighth (coral) squares grey; text '6 of 8 boxes shared'. A small grey note by the orange tab: 'other Cathartes species not shown'. Counter: 'boxes: 7'.
scenes.narration: No. Among our seven, the genus box closes around the turkey vulture alone. The black vulture belongs to a different genus, called Coragyps. It shares six boxes with the turkey vulture, not seven.

scenes.tts: The last of our eight main boxes is the species. A species is a group of similar living things that can mate in nature. Their young can also reproduce. This is a useful rule for many living things that reproduce with sex cells. It has limits.
scenes.visual: A CORAL RED box closes snugly around the turkey vulture; tab '8 SPECIES: Cathartes aura'. Beside it, two turkey vultures and a fledgling appear in a small inset nest, labelled 'can mate in nature, young can also reproduce'. A small grey note below: 'a useful rule, with limits'. Counter: 'boxes: 8'.
scenes.narration: The last of our eight main boxes is the species. A species is a group of similar living things that can mate in nature. Their young can also reproduce. This is a useful rule for many living things that reproduce with sex cells. It has limits.

scenes.tts: The genus box is labelled Ka-thar-teez. Add a second word, aura, and you have the species name, Ka-thar-teez aura.
scenes.caption: The genus box is labelled Cathartes. Add a second word, aura, and you have the species name, Cathartes aura.
scenes.visual: Camera zooms in on the orange and coral tabs. The orange tab reads 'Cathartes', labelled 'genus name'. The word 'aura' writes itself after it, labelled 'second word'. The coral tab reads the whole name, 'Cathartes aura', in italics, with a bracket under both words labelled 'species name'. The coral tab never shows 'aura' alone.
scenes.narration: The genus box is labelled Cathartes. Add a second word, aura, and you have the species name, Cathartes aura.

scenes.tts: The genus gets a capital letter, and the second word is lowercase. Print both words in italics, or underline both by hand. A scientist in Japan who writes Ka-thar-teez aura means the same bird you see in Virginia.
scenes.caption: The genus gets a capital letter, and the second word is lowercase. Print both words in italics, or underline both by hand. A scientist in Japan who writes Cathartes aura means the same bird you see in Virginia.
scenes.visual: The name 'Cathartes aura' sits large on screen. A pointer circles the capital C and the lowercase a. The italic text then appears again below, handwritten, with both words underlined. A small globe spins: a speech bubble from Japan and one from Virginia both show 'Cathartes aura' and point to the same turkey vulture.
scenes.narration: The genus gets a capital letter, and the second word is lowercase. Print both words in italics, or underline both by hand. A scientist in Japan who writes Cathartes aura means the same bird you see in Virginia.

scenes.tts: The bird people in Britain call a buzzard has its own name, Byoo-tee-oh byoo-tee-oh. Two names, two birds, no mix up.
scenes.caption: The bird people in Britain call a buzzard has its own name, Buteo buteo. Two names, two birds, no mix up.
scenes.visual: Split screen. Left: the turkey vulture with 'Cathartes aura' under it. Right: the brown British hawk with 'Buteo buteo' under it. The word 'buzzard' floats between them, then fades out. No boxes are compared on this screen.
scenes.narration: The bird people in Britain call a buzzard has its own name, Buteo buteo. Two names, two birds, no mix up.

scenes.tts: The black vulture stayed in for six, and the hawk left sooner. The more boxes two living things share, the more closely they are grouped. Scientists can redraw a box when they learn more.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the full nested picture, navy to coral, with every living thing resting where it left. The black vulture's tally strip shows 6 lit squares; the hawk's shows 5. A rule card slides up: 'More shared boxes = grouped more closely.' One box wall shimmers and shifts slightly, labelled 'walls can move when scientists learn more (schematic)'. Small grey note: 'eight main boxes, one classification'.
scenes.narration: The black vulture stayed in for six, and the hawk left sooner. The more boxes two living things share, the more closely they are grouped. Scientists can redraw a box when they learn more.

scenes.visual: End card: the hexagon mascot Hex holds a small nested-box sign in navy to coral. Line on screen: 'The more boxes two living things share, the more closely they're grouped.'
